subject: chemistry-1
question: Sodium chloride melts near 801 degrees C, while methane melts near -182 degrees C, a difference of 983 degrees C. What is the primary reason for this very large gap?

options.text: Melting sodium chloride breaks a lattice of strong ion-ion attractions, while melting methane overcomes only weak intermolecular forces.
Melting methane breaks the strong C-H covalent bonds inside each molecule, while melting sodium chloride leaves its ionic bonds fully intact.
Melting sodium chloride overcomes many weak attractions that add up, while melting methane breaks one unusually strong covalent bond.
Sodium chloride is built from much heavier atoms than methane, so far more thermal energy is needed to set its particles moving.

explanation:
In an ionic solid each ion is attracted to every oppositely charged neighbor throughout a continuous three-dimensional array, so melting must supply enough energy to overcome a large lattice energy. Methane is a molecular solid whose discrete molecules are held to one another only by weak London dispersion forces; melting separates the molecules while the strong C-H covalent bonds inside each molecule remain untouched. Option B reverses which particles come apart, option C wrongly treats the ionic lattice as a stack of weak additive attractions and methane as having a single covalent bond, and option D misattributes the gap to atomic mass rather than to the type of force being broken.

ELI-10: Melting always asks the same question: what has to let go for particles to start sliding past each other? In sodium chloride the answer is full positive-negative attractions running through the whole crystal, which is a lot to overcome. In methane the answer is only the faint stickiness between separate molecules; the bonds inside each CH4 stay put. Weak attractions give way at -182 degrees C, strong ionic ones not until 801 degrees C, a melting temperature 983 degrees C higher.
